turns.doctor_question: When you were younger, did you have trouble understanding other people’s social cues or making/keeping friendships?
turns.patient_response:
When I was younger? No, not really. I mean, I had friends, I understood things fine. I don't remember any particular trouble with social cues. 

Social cues are actually an incredibly inefficient data transmission protocol if you think about it. The bandwidth is so low, and the signal-to-noise ratio is terrible. People rely on micro-expressions, right? A slight tightening of the orbicularis oculi muscle to indicate a genuine smile, a Duchenne smile, versus a polite, fabricated one. But the visual processing required to decode that in real-time is immense. It's why I've always preferred asynchronous text-based communication. The parameters are defined. You have an ASCII character set, or Unicode if you're dealing with special symbols, and the parsing rules are standardized. 

I remember when Unicode first started gaining traction. Before that, you had all these conflicting character encodings. ISO 8859-1 for Western European languages, Shift JIS for Japanese. If a file was saved in the wrong encoding, you'd open it and just get this massive string of mojibake—completely corrupted characters. It was a nightmare for database integrity. You'd have to write these elaborate regex scripts just to scrub the data and map the byte sequences back to the correct glyphs. Regular expressions are beautiful, really. It's pure finite state machine logic. You can condense hundreds of lines of string manipulation code into a single, elegant string of syntax. 

I spent a whole summer once writing a regex parser from scratch in C. C is such an unforgiving language. It doesn't hold your hand with memory management. If you don't explicitly free the memory you allocate on the heap with malloc, you get a memory leak, and eventually, the operating system just kills your process. The garbage collection in modern languages like Python or Java makes people lazy. They don't understand the underlying architecture of the von Neumann machine they're working on. The CPU registers, the L1 and L2 cache hierarchies... 

But, um... sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, when I was younger. No, I didn't have any issues making friends or anything like that.

Hearing voices? No, no, nothing like that. I don't hear anything that isn't there. 

Sound is just mechanical waves, anyway. Longitudinal waves propagating through a medium, usually air, at roughly 343 meters per second, depending on the ambient temperature and humidity. The human auditory system is really only calibrated for about 20 Hertz to 20 kilohertz, though obviously that upper limit degrades significantly by the time you reach my age. The stereocilia in the cochlea—the tiny hair cells that translate the vibrations—they just suffer from mechanical fatigue over time. It's a fascinating structural failure, really. 

I was actually looking into the math behind acoustic metamaterials last month before... well, before the interference on my projects started. You can engineer lattice structures at the sub-wavelength scale to actually bend sound waves around an object. It effectively creates an acoustic cloak. It uses the exact same mathematical principles as optical metamaterials with negative refractive indices, just applied to phononics instead of light. The Navy is incredibly interested in it for submarine stealth. Traditional active sonar relies on acoustic backscatter, so if you can channel the pressure waves completely around the hull, you're mathematically invisible. Right now they just use anechoic tiles, those thick rubber coatings, but they are terribly inefficient at low frequencies because the wavelengths are just too massive. A 50 Hertz sound wave in seawater is about 30 meters long. You can't absorb a 30-meter wave with a two-inch piece of rubber, it completely defies basic physics. You'd need active noise cancellation, generating an inverse wave exactly 180 degrees out of phase to create perfect destructive interference... 

But, um... wait. What did you ask me? Oh. Voices, right. Right. No, I don't hear any voices. Just the normal ambient noise in the room.

turns.doctor_question: Have you also had a period of several days or more when your mood was unusually elevated or very irritable?
turns.patient_response:
Elevated? Or irritable? No, I wouldn't say that. My mood is fairly constant, really. It stays pretty stable. 

Stability is actually an incredibly difficult state to maintain in any dynamic system, though. You almost always need a closed-loop feedback mechanism to achieve it. Like a PID controller—Proportional, Integral, Derivative. The proportional band handles the immediate error between your current state and your setpoint, but if you rely entirely on that, you always end up with a steady-state error. An offset. So you have to introduce the integral term to sum the error over time and force the system to the target. But if your integral gain is too high, the system overshoots wildly. I suppose you could mathematically model an "elevated mood" as an integral overshoot. And the derivative term, that dampens the rate of change. If you tune the derivative incorrectly, the system becomes hyper-reactive to high-frequency noise. It gets incredibly jittery. Extremely irritable, you might say. 

I actually spent three weeks trying to tune the PID loop for a custom extrusion nozzle on a 3D printer I was modifying a while back. The thermistor was picking up electromagnetic interference from the stepper motors, so the temperature readings were fluctuating by tiny fractions of a degree, but the derivative algorithm was overcompensating for the noise. The temperature just kept oscillating. I finally had to solder a low-pass RC filter directly onto the mainboard—just a simple resistor and capacitor in series—to smooth out the analog signal before it hit the analog-to-digital converter. It's basic signal processing, really, but the manufacturer completely overlooked it just to save maybe three cents on the bill of materials. It is absolutely astonishing how corners get cut in modern consumer electronics. Just the parasitic capacitance of the copper traces on the PCB alone can completely degrade a low-voltage signal if you don't route them orthogonally to the power lines... 

But, um... wait, what were you asking me about? Oh, right. My mood. No, I don't get elevated or irritable like that. Just... baseline, I suppose.

Less sleep? And full of energy? No, I don't think so. I get my usual amount of rest. Sleep is just a basic biological requirement for clearing out metabolic waste, really. 

It’s an entropy problem, if you look at it mathematically. The brain is trying to decrease local entropy during those cycles, which obviously requires a constant metabolic baseline. It’s exactly like a refrigerator—you can’t just magically make the inside cold, you have to pump the thermal energy out into the surrounding environment, so the total entropy of the universe still increases. The Second Law of Thermodynamics is completely inescapable. I was actually trying to model neural energy states a while back using spin glass theory. It’s a beautiful application of statistical mechanics. You use a Hamiltonian function to map out the minimum energy configurations, but the issue with spin glasses is that the system constantly gets trapped in local minima. It’s a classic non-convex optimization problem. You have to introduce a stochastic variable, like simulated annealing, to randomly bump the system out of that local valley so it can find the true global minimum. 

Simulated annealing is actually borrowed directly from metallurgy. You heat a metal until the atoms have high kinetic energy, and then you cool it down incredibly slowly so they form a perfect crystalline lattice. If you drop the temperature too fast—quenching—you just freeze all the microscopic structural defects in place, and the material becomes hopelessly brittle. I actually built a small induction forge in my garage a few years ago to test this with scrap aluminum, but the inductive load was so massive it kept tripping the 20-amp breaker on my subpanel. I had to sit down and recalculate the exact impedance of the copper work coils using complex phasors just to figure out the phase angle between the voltage and the current... 

But, ah, wait. What were we talking about? Energy? Oh, right, sleeping. No, I don't go days without sleep. I definitely need my rest.

Light rays striking the outer edge of a spherical mirror converge at a completely different focal point than the rays hitting the center, so the image gets hopelessly blurred. You really need a parabolic mirror to fix it, but grinding a perfect parabola is a massive non-linear manufacturing problem. turns.doctor_question: Have you generally felt this way for as long as you can remember, or is this mostly a change from how you used to be?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, it's definitely a change. I haven't always been like this. This whole decline really started after I was put in charge of the larger environmental modeling contract... that was about two years and two months ago, I think. 

Environmental modeling is just incredibly computationally expensive. You’re dealing with massive, non-linear partial differential equations across huge spatial grids. If you look at the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid dynamics—which govern all the atmospheric and oceanic currents—they don’t even have a proven general analytical solution. It’s one of the Millennium Prize problems. You have to discretize the entire spatial domain using finite volume methods and solve it numerically. I was setting up a computational fluid dynamics simulation to model atmospheric particulate dispersion, and the sheer volume of floating-point operations required was just staggering. We had to lease time on a high-performance computing cluster. 

But the latency between the computing nodes was causing a massive bottleneck because the facility was using standard gigabit Ethernet instead of an InfiniBand architecture. InfiniBand is a beautifully elegant solution because it bypasses the operating system kernel entirely. It allows direct remote memory access between servers, which drops your latency down to just a couple of microseconds. It’s exactly the kind of hardware optimization you need when you're passing boundary condition matrices back and forth millions of times a second. I actually spent a whole weekend drafting a proposal to upgrade our local server rack with some decommissioned InfiniBand switches I found online, but the thermal dissipation requirements for the transceivers were completely incompatible with our HVAC setup. You really need a hot-aisle containment system to manage the airflow efficiently, otherwise the ambient temperature in the server room just creeps up exponentially...

But, um... wait, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? How long I've felt like this? Right. Yeah, it hasn't been forever. Just since I took on that larger modeling contract, about two years and two months ago. That's when things really started to change for me.

turns.doctor_question: Do other people usually find it hard to follow your speech because you jump from one idea to another or lose your train of thought?
turns.patient_response:
Hard to follow? No, I don't think so. I've never had anyone tell me that. I actually try to be extremely precise with my vocabulary. 

Precision in language is really just an extension of precision in mathematics, if you think about it. You need a rigorously defined syntax to avoid ambiguity. It’s exactly like designing a compiler for a programming language. You have to define the lexical grammar using regular expressions first, and then you parse those tokens into an abstract syntax tree. The AST is a beautifully elegant hierarchical data structure. It’s fundamentally just a directed acyclic graph. Graph theory is absolutely fascinating once you dig into it. Leonhard Euler basically invented it in the 18th century just to solve the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem. He mathematically proved that a continuous path crossing every bridge exactly once only exists if every landmass—or vertex—has an even number of bridges connected to it, with at most two exceptions. It’s a strict topological invariant. 

I actually spent a few months trying to map out the entire US interstate highway system using graph theory. I wanted to calculate the absolute most efficient route for a road trip I was planning down to the Very Large Array in New Mexico. The VLA is an incredible piece of engineering. It uses 27 independent radio antennas arranged in a massive Y-pattern on railroad tracks. They use aperture synthesis and interferometry to combine the signals, which effectively creates a single radio telescope with a resolving power equivalent to a dish 22 miles across. But to do that, you have to account for the exact speed-of-light delay between each individual antenna using hydrogen maser atomic clocks. If your timing is off by even a fraction of a nanosecond, the phase coherence of the incoming radio waves is completely destroyed and all your data just turns into Gaussian noise... 

But, ah... wait. What were we talking about? Losing my train of thought? Oh. No, I don't think I do that. My communication is perfectly logical, so people usually understand me just fine.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly denies losing their train of thought or having hard-to-follow speech, but simultaneously demonstrates severe tangentiality, derailment, and literally loses their train of thought during the response.

turns.doctor_question: When you were younger and in your teens or early adulthood, did you also tend to prefer being alone and keep a lot of distance from other people?
turns.patient_response:
No, not at all. When I was younger, like in my late teens and early twenties, I was actually very social. I had a really tight-knit study group in college when I was taking my first numerical analysis courses. We used to spend hours and hours together in the computer lab. 

Back then, we were working on these early VAX machines—the VAX-11/780, specifically. It was a 32-bit complex instruction set computer, and the instruction set architecture was just incredibly orthogonal. That means you could use basically any addressing mode with any instruction, which made assembly programming so much more intuitive compared to the x86 architecture that ended up dominating the market later on. x86 is really just a tangled mess of legacy microcode if you look at it closely. But the memory management on the VAX was what was truly fascinating. It used virtual memory with demand paging, which was a huge deal at the time. The page tables were structured hierarchically to map virtual addresses to physical frames in the RAM. If a page wasn't in main memory, the CPU would generate a page fault interrupt, and the operating system had to halt and fetch it from the hard drive. And hard drives back then were these massive, heavy platter arrays. The read/write heads had to physically seek across the platters, which introduces a massive amount of mechanical latency. You always had to calculate the rotational delay—the exact time it takes for the correct data sector to spin under the magnetic head. If you didn't optimize your disk I/O scheduling using something like the elevator algorithm, the mechanical seeking would cause disk thrashing, and the whole system would just crawl to a halt. Thrashing is an interesting state where the system spends exponentially more time paging data in and out of memory than it does actually executing any useful instructions... 

But, um... wait, I'm sorry. What were we talking about? My teens? Oh, right. No, I didn't keep my distance back then. I was always in the lab with the other guys. We were a good group. I never really wanted to be isolated until recently.
